bank.finding: The message has no link to click and no phone number to call. It does not ask for money, a password, a code, or your card number.
It only asks you to reply YES or NO, and says Chase will never ask for your password. This matches how real Chase fraud alert texts work.
Real Chase fraud texts usually show the last 4 digits of your card. This message does not. That's not proof of a scam, but it's worth checking with Chase yourself.
Some scammers send a YES/NO text like this and then call pretending to be Chase. A real Chase worker will never ask for your password, a code, or ask you to move money.

Chase's official website lists its fraud phone numbers: 1-800-935-9935 (option 8) for checking accounts and debit cards, and 1-800-955-9060 (option 2) for personal credit cards. The number on the back of your card also works.

verdict.headline: This looks like a real Chase fraud alert. To be sure, call the number on the back of your card.
reasons: There is no link, no phone number, and no request for money, a password, or a code.
It only asks YES or NO, which is how real Chase fraud alerts work.
One small worry: real Chase texts usually show the last 4 digits of your card, and this one does not.
nextSteps: If you have a Chase card and you made this Target purchase, you can reply YES. If you didn't make it, reply NO, or don't reply at all and call Chase instead.
To be completely sure, call the number on the back of your Chase card, or call 1-800-935-9935 (debit) or 1-800-955-9060 (credit card).
If someone calls you after this text saying they are from Chase, hang up. Then call the number on the back of your card yourself.
Never give anyone a password, a code sent by text, or your full card number, and never move money to a "safe" account.

usps.label: Reading the message for warning signs

usps.finding: The Postal Inspection Service says USPS does not text you unless you asked for updates with a tracking number, and its texts will NOT contain a link. This text has a link and no tracking number.
This matches a well-known scam text: "package on hold because of an incomplete address." It is widely reported as a trick to steal card and personal details.
The message rushes you with a 12-hour deadline. Scammers use deadlines so you act before you think.
Some of our checks did not work this time: we could not see when the website was made, where the link leads, or whether it is on scam lists. These failed checks prove nothing either way.
The real USPS phone number is 1-800-275-8777 (1-800-ASK-USPS). The real website is usps.com.

verdict.headline: This is a scam. Do not click the link.
reasons: The link goes to a fake website (usps-redeliver-help.xyz) that copies the USPS name. The real USPS website is usps.com.
USPS says its texts never contain a link, and it only texts you if you asked for updates with a tracking number.
This is a well-known scam text about a package "on hold" for an "incomplete address," with a rush deadline to make you hurry.
nextSteps: Do not click the link or reply to the text.
Delete the text. You can forward it to 7726 (SPAM) to report it to your phone company.
If you are expecting a package, check it yourself at usps.com or call USPS at 1-800-275-8777.
If you already clicked and typed in card details, call your bank using the number on the back of your card.

jail.finding: The message asks for $2,000 in gift cards. Real jails, courts, and lawyers never take bail or fees in gift cards. Only scammers ask for this.
It says "don't tell mom." Scammers ask for secrecy so you won't check with family and find out the truth.
This matches the well-known "grandparent scam" word for word: a grandchild in jail, an urgent need for money, and a plea to keep it secret. The FTC warns about this exact trick.
The sender never says their name. "It's me" lets the scammer get you to say a grandchild's name for them.
The message has no link or phone number for us to check. The words alone are enough to show it is a scam.

verdict.headline: This is a scam. Do not buy or send any gift cards.
reasons: It asks for $2,000 in gift cards. Real jails and lawyers never take payment in gift cards.
It says "don't tell mom." Scammers ask for secrecy so you won't check with family.
It follows the well-known "grandparent scam" that the FTC warns about: a grandchild in jail who needs money fast.
nextSteps: Do not reply and do not buy any gift cards.
Call your grandchild on the phone number you already have for them, or call their mom or dad.
If anyone asks for money again, hang up and talk to a family member you trust first.
You can report the message to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Pide guardar el secreto ("no le digas a mamá"). Los estafadores piden esto para que usted no pueda confirmar la historia con la familia.
El mensaje no dice el nombre de la persona: solo "soy yo". Es la frase típica de la "estafa del nieto": un supuesto familiar en problemas que pide dinero urgente.
La Comisión Federal de Comercio (FTC) de EE. UU. advierte sobre esta misma estafa: un "nieto" que dice estar en la cárcel, pide dinero y pide guardar el secreto.
El mensaje no trae enlaces ni números de teléfono para revisar.

verdict.headline: Esto es una estafa. No compre tarjetas de regalo ni mande dinero.
reasons: Pide $2,000 en tarjetas de regalo. Ninguna cárcel ni abogado cobra así, y ese dinero casi nunca se recupera.
Pide guardar el secreto ("no le digas a mamá") para que usted no pueda confirmar la historia.
Es la conocida "estafa del nieto": no dice su nombre, solo "soy yo", y cuenta una emergencia para asustarla.
nextSteps: No conteste el mensaje y no compre ninguna tarjeta de regalo.
Llame a su nieto o nieta al número que usted ya tiene guardado de antes.

alert.summary: Your family member got a message that looked like it was from a grandchild: "Grandma it's me, I'm in jail, please send $2,000 in gift cards, don't tell mom." This is a well-known grandparent scam. She has already sent one $500 gift card.
alert.suggestedAction: Please call her now. Tell her the grandchild is safe and help her call the gift card company to freeze the $500. Make sure she sends no more money, then help her report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

steps.title: Do not send any more gift cards
steps.detail: This trick fools many careful people. You did the right thing by checking. Please do not send the other $1,500, and do not reply to the message. If they write or call again, hang up or ignore it.

steps.title: Call the gift card company right now
steps.detail: Look on the back of the gift card or the card holder for the company's phone number, or go to the company's official website. Tell them the card was used in a scam and ask them to freeze the money. If the scammer has not spent it yet, you may get it back. Have the card number and receipt ready.

steps.title: Keep the card and the receipt
steps.detail: Keep the gift card, its packaging, and the store receipt. These prove what you bought and help the company find the money. Don't throw anything away.

steps.title: Call your grandchild on the number you already have
steps.detail: Use the phone number you already know is theirs, not one from the message. Or call their mom or dad. You will most likely find out they are safe and not in jail.

steps.title: Save the message
steps.detail: Don't delete the message. Take a picture of it or a screenshot. Write down the date and time it came and who it came from.

steps.title: Report it
steps.detail: Report what happened to the FTC and the FBI. This helps stop the scammers and can help if you need to get your money back. You can use the reports below.

steps.title: Expect more tricks
steps.detail: Scammers often come back pretending to be a lawyer, police officer, or someone who can 'get your money back'. Anyone who asks for more money or gift cards is part of the scam.
